problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}+6y=30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x},
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-6x}$, find the particular solution to the equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x},$ and ${e}^{-6x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, while ${e}^{x}$ is not, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-6x})^{′}+\beta ({e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-6x}-6x{e}^{-6x})+\beta {e}^{x} \\  & =\alpha (1-6x){e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-6x){e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x})+6(\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x}) & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x} \\ (1-6x+6x)\alpha {e}^{-6x}+(\beta +6\beta ){e}^{x} & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-6x}+7\beta {e}^{x} & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of ${e}^{-6x}$ and ${e}^{x}$ gives

$$
\alpha =30\,\text{and}\,7\beta =4,
$$

so, we have

$$
\alpha =30\,\text{and}\,\beta =\frac{4}{7}.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=30x{e}^{-6x}+\frac{4}{7}{e}^{x}.
$$
